definition: Production inputs departing from training-time distributions (drift) or the input-output relationship itself changing (concept drift): new slang, new products, new attack patterns.
details: Production inputs departing from training-time distributions (drift) or the input-output relationship itself changing (concept drift): new slang, new products, new attack patterns. The reason deployed models decay and monitoring exists; detected via input statistics, embedding distributions, and rolling eval scores.

explainer.lead: Data drift is what happens when the data a deployed model sees stops resembling the data it learned from. It can quietly make predictions worse, which is why production models need ongoing monitoring rather than a one-time accuracy check.

tiers.eli5: Imagine learning to identify animals from a book full of farm pictures, then being taken to a zoo. The animals look different from your examples, so you may make more mistakes. Data drift is the model version of that surprise, and monitoring is how people notice it.
tiers.practitioner: Teams monitor input statistics and embedding distributions for departures from training-time data, and track rolling evaluation scores for signs of decay. These checks fit language applications facing new slang, catalogs gaining new products, and security systems facing new attack patterns. A pitfall is treating a distribution alert as proof of failure: input drift and a changed input-output relationship are not the same thing.
tiers.paperLevel: Input drift can be written as P_t(X) differing from P_train(X), while concept drift means P_t(Y|X) differs from P_train(Y|X). The first changes what inputs occur; the second changes the relationship the model must predict. Monitoring can use input statistics, embedding distributions, and rolling evaluation scores, but a change in inputs alone does not establish that predictive performance has fallen.

explainer.example: A detector trained on older attack messages starts receiving a new attack pattern. Its input statistics and embedding distribution shift away from training data, and its rolling evaluation score falls, alerting the team that the deployed model is decaying.

usedIn.name: Language applications
usedIn.detail: New slang can make production text differ from training text.

usedIn.name: Product catalogs
usedIn.detail: New products introduce inputs that an existing model may not represent well.

usedIn.name: Security systems
usedIn.detail: New attack patterns can shift both incoming data and evaluation results.

explainer.intuition: A model learns patterns from a snapshot of the world, but production data keeps moving. When the inputs change, or when the same inputs begin to imply different outputs, yesterday's patterns can become less reliable.
howItWorks: Record the distributions and behavior represented by the training data.
Deploy the model and observe its production inputs.
Compare input statistics and embedding distributions with their training-time counterparts.
Track rolling evaluation scores to detect declining performance.
Distinguish changed inputs from a changed input-output relationship, known as concept drift.
explainer.whyItMatters: Drift explains why a model that tested well before deployment can become less accurate afterward. Monitoring makes that decay visible so teams are not relying on stale assumptions about production data.
misconceptions: Data drift is not limited to changed inputs; concept drift concerns the input-output relationship itself.
A shift in input distributions does not by itself prove that accuracy has dropped.
Passing pre-deployment evaluation does not remove the need for production monitoring.

diagram.caption: Production monitoring compares changing inputs with training-time distributions and tracks model scores over time.
